summary: A first-person travelogue on creation myths from many cultures, begun September 1, 2023, drawing on interviews and visits to festivals and sites from the Andes to Alice Springs. It groups myths by theme (sound, artistry, water, celestial, serpent, rebirth) and stresses the role of oral tradition. It concludes that these myths share a universal human quest for meaning and belonging.
one_line: A travel-based exploration of world creation myths and oral tradition, finding a shared human search for meaning across cultures.
key_facts: The author began the journey of collecting creation tales on September 1, 2023.
Folklorist Dr. Emily Rosenthal, who has spent the better part of the last decade on these narratives, says "Creation myths are the cultural DNA of a society."
On October 15, 2023, the author attended an annual festival in a remote Andes village celebrating Pachamama, the earth mother who nurtures all life.
Among the Bantu people, the god Mbombo is said to have vomited forth the world and all life within it.
Nigerian historian Adebowale Okeke said at a Lagos symposium on November 20, 2023: "Without orality, there's no memory. And without memory, there is no identity."
In Norse myth, Odin and his brothers fashion the world from the carcass of the giant Ymir, born from the chaos of fire and ice.
On December 3, 2023, in Uppsala, Sweden, the author observed rituals in which effigies symbolizing the old and new were burned and created.

Pacific Northwest First Nations tell of a great flood and renewal of life by a raven; the Haida Nation, visited in British Columbia on January 22, 2024, express gratitude to the raven and have totem poles.
In Ancient Egypt, the god Atum is believed to have created himself, emerging from the primeval waters; the author toured Giza on February 10, 2024.
In Aboriginal Australian lore the Rainbow Serpent creates land formations and life sources; elders told its story in Alice Springs on March 5, 2024.
At Persepolis in Iran on April 2, 2024, storytellers recounted tales of the Simurgh, the Persian equivalent of the phoenix, a symbol of rebirth.
The author concludes that creation myths across cultures reflect a shared quest for meaning and a need to belong to something greater.
